```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>"
)
if (requireNamespace("ragg", quietly = TRUE)) {
  # Render figures through ragg so bundled fonts resolve identically on
  # every platform.
  knitr::opts_chunk$set(dev = "ragg_png")
}
```

This guide will walk you through the themes and tools available in the `ojothemes` package. We'll start by loading the package (plus `ojodb` for some test data), then we'll make some example graphs and tables to show you what's available.

```{r setup}
library(ojothemes)
library(ojodb)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(lubridate)
library(gt)

# Test data from OCDC
data <- ojo_tbl(
  schema = "ocdc",
  table = "arrest"
) |>
  filter(
    book_date >= "01-01-2024",
    book_date < "11-01-2024"
  ) |>
  ojo_collect()
```

## Themes for `ggplot` graphs

First, let's see how this data looks on a default ggplot:

```{r default_ggplot}
p1 <- data |>
  # We'll look at the bookings by race here,
  # and we'll look by month just to make it easier to see.
  count(
    book_month = floor_date(book_date, "months"),
    race
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = book_month, y = n, fill = race)) +
  geom_col() +
  # When a legend has many categories, wrap it in rows so it doesn't
  # overflow the plot
  guides(fill = guide_legend(nrow = 3))

p1
```

Next, let's gussy this up with our `ojothemes` tools. First, let's use the `ojothemes::ojo_labs()` function to easily add a nice caption to the plot:

```{r ojo_labs}
p1 <- p1 +
  ojo_labs(
    analyst_name = "Andrew Bell",
    source = "ocdc",
    title = "OCDC Bookings by Race",
    subtitle = "January 2024 - October 2024",
    x = "Month",
    y = "Total Booking Events"
  )

p1
```

This is just a wrapper for the normal `ggplot2::labs()` function, so we can pass arguments like `title`, `subtitle`, `x`, and `y` to it. The really neat thing, though, is the new `analyst_name` and `source` arguments. These will add a nice little "Graphic created by..." caption crediting the analyst, and a consistently phrased note on where the data came from.

  * Right now, you can use `"oscn"`, `"ocdc"`, or `"ppb"` as the `source` argument to get a pre-written, consistent source note. However, if you're working with something not in one of those domains, you can just tell it something to put in there verbatim, e.g. `source = "Source: Data Pulled from The National Insitute of My Ass database"`.

Next, let's actually apply our themes. There are two ways to do this: the first is to just throw `+ theme_opi()` onto our ggplot, like so:

```{r plus_theme_opi}
p1 + theme_opi()
```

This applies not just the theme / fonts, but the color / fill scales as well. If you want just the theme without the scales, you can do `p1 + theme_opi_base()`.

The second way of applying a theme is by using `ojothemes::ojo_set_theme()`. This is probably going to be the most common way of doing things, since we're rarely going to want to use multiple themes in the same script / document / etc. Let's try that same graph in the "tok" theme this time:

```{r set_theme_tok}
ojo_set_theme(theme = "tok")

p1
```

## Themes for `gt` tables

This package also has built in themes for tables made with `gt`. You can use these by replacing the normal `gt()` function with our themed wrapper `gt_opi()`. It has built in arguments for customization:

  * `source` and `analyst_name` (which work just like the `ojo_labs()` function for ggplots)
  * `title` and `subtitle` (self explanatory)
  * `format_cols` (a logical that will apply the auto-styling from `gt` to every column if `TRUE`)
  * `font_size` for making really big / small tables.

Here's what a normal, unstyled table looks like...

```{r gt}
data |>
  count(race) |>
  gt()
```

...and here's what our `gt_opi()` theme does to it...

```{r gt_opi}
data |>
  count(race) |>
  gt_opi(
    title = "OCDC Bookings by Race",
    subtitle = "January 2024 - October 2024",
    source = "ocdc",
    analyst_name = "Andrew Bell",
    format_cols = TRUE
  )
```

## Fonts

`ojothemes` takes care of fonts for you. **Source Sans 3** ships inside the
package and is registered with `systemfonts` at load time — no font
installation, admin rights, or network access is ever needed. Every theme
defaults to it, so plots render pixel-identically on Windows, macOS, and
Linux.

To see where each font known to ojothemes resolves from on your machine,
run:

```{r ojo_fonts}
ojo_fonts()
```

The `source` column tells you where each family comes from:

  * `bundled` — shipped inside the package; always available, identical on every machine
  * `local` — found in a `fonts/` folder in your project (or `~/fonts`)
  * `fetched` — downloaded and cached by `systemfonts` on first use
  * `system` — installed on the operating system
  * `missing` — not found; plots using it will fall back to a default font

### Using proprietary fonts (e.g. Adobe Myriad Pro)

Fonts that can't be redistributed (like Myriad Pro) can't be bundled in the
package, but they still work through the same machinery: copy your licensed
`.otf`/`.ttf` files into a `fonts/` folder in your project and `systemfonts`
will pick them up automatically — no OS installation needed. Check
`ojo_fonts()` afterwards; `Myriad Pro` should show `local`.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# e.g. fonts/Myriad Pro Regular.ttf, Myriad Pro Bold.ttf, ...
ojo_fonts()
```

Note that Source Sans 3 (bundled, and free to redistribute) is drawn in the
same Adobe type program as Myriad and is nearly glyph-identical, running
about 3-5% optically smaller at the same point size. For fully
self-contained, reproducible work, prefer Source Sans 3 unless the brand
requires Myriad Pro.

## Exporting plots

Use `ojo_save_png()` and `ojo_save_svg()` to export plots. They always
render through `ragg` / `svglite` (so bundled fonts resolve identically on
every platform) and accept dimensions in any unit, so specs from the
communications team can be passed verbatim:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# inches (physical)
ojo_save_png(p1, "bookings.png", width = 7, height = 5, unit = "in")

# pixels, dpi-relative (here: 1080 px at 144 dpi = 7.5 in)
ojo_save_png(p1, "bookings.png", width = 1080, height = 675, unit = "px", dpi = 144)

# points, absolute physical units (1 pt = 1/72 in)
ojo_save_png(p1, "bookings.png", width = 504, height = 360, unit = "pt")

# millimeters, and SVG (vector; resolution-independent)
ojo_save_png(p1, "bookings.png", width = 178, height = 127, unit = "mm")
ojo_save_svg(p1, "bookings.svg", width = 178, height = 127, unit = "mm")
```

Notes:

  * `unit = "px"` without `dpi` defaults to 72 dpi (the graphics device
    convention: 1 px = 1/72 in). If a pixel spec was authored for a
    different resolution, pass it explicitly.
  * String dpi aliases like `"retina"` are rejected on purpose — pass the
    explicit number the spec was authored for.
  * Export always uses ragg/svglite (never the base devices), so the same
    command produces pixel-identical output on Windows, macOS, and Linux.
